extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novice to intermediate), especially novelists and short-story authors looking for structural techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on using a concrete 'thing' (map, place, date, object, game, etc.) as the organizing structure for a story, with examples, benefits, and cautions for implementation. Targets writers seeking techniques to pace, outline, and constrain their narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring around a map/place/location
rubrics_metrics.description: Build the story around a map or location (e.g., everyone contained within a spaceship, a building, a tower) so the geography becomes the organizing principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A map or fixed location 'tells the reader where you are going' and gives the writer an automatic outline; examples include The Lord of the Rings (starts in the Shire), Die Hard and its countless location-based clones, and the Tower of Babel books (Senlin Ascends) where each level is a chapter/section. Benefits: makes the story relatable (readers know how buildings/places function) and forces creative problem-solving within constraints. Anti-pattern: when each chapter is a new location, you may need to flesh out those locations more; otherwise the chapter can feel lazy or unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring around a date/countdown
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a date or built-in countdown as the primary structural device so pacing is driven by a known endpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A countdown provides automatic pacing and natural propulsion toward the end; it helps keep timelines correct and sets reader expectations early (Dan's 'Makeover' example where every chapter begins with a countdown to the end of the world). Caution: telling readers the endgame up front can alter their expectations (not a spoiler if set up intentionally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring around a game/ruleset/tutorial progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a game, rule set, or tutorial-like learning progression as the framework for the story, where each stage adds complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: structuring like boardgame tutorial levels or videogame power/life systems (Jumanji, recent Jumanji films). This allows gradual introduction of mechanics, abilities, or complexity (a natural way to increase stakes and teach readers 'rules'). Use it to slowly increase complexity over time. It functions well as an outline and pacing device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring around an artifact/object (puzzle as plot scaffold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Center the narrative on an object or artifact that contains structure or puzzle elements (e.g., a chess game depicted in a painting that encodes a mystery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Flanders Panel uses the chess game as the organizing device with diagrams of moves between chapters so readers can follow. An object can provide an internal logic and a clear end condition (when the game/ puzzle is solved, the story climaxes). This is addictive for readers who can follow the device; it gives the writer concrete beats to hit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadly-maze or progressive-penetration structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the story as progressive descent/penetration through levels of a place or artifact (each segment goes deeper into the thing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic examples include 'deadly maze' SF like Diamond Dogs and elements in Piranesi. Each segment/chapter represents a deeper layer or new interior space, creating escalating stakes and discovery. This imposes physical constraints that shape plot choices and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structure as an automatic outline (helps pantsers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt an external 'thing' structure when you don't plan extensively— the thing provides an implied outline to guide writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly helpful for 'pantsers' who don't pre-outline; structuring around location, time, or objects gives a scaffold so you know the end goal or next beat (e.g., Tower of Babel: get to the top). This reduces paralysis about what comes next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make constraints work creatively and increase relatability
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage the built-in limitations of the 'thing' (space, rules, artifact constraints) to force inventive solutions and make scenarios relatable to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraints (e.g., characters stuck in a building) simplify choices for characters and push creative problem-solving, which can heighten tension and engage readers. Example: Die Hard's single-building constraint made the film easy to follow and spawned many 'Die Hard on X' variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flesh out locations/structural elements so they feel necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When each chapter/segment is a new location or module, ensure the location is sufficiently developed to justify its inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: having a chapter solely because 'this is where this piece of the plot happens' but not making the place feel real. If a location is only a convenience, readers may feel the chapter is lazy—either deepen the locale or combine/relocate the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structural devices to pace character introductions and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the structure (e.g., modules unpacking, floors of a tower) determine when new characters/agents arrive so the cast and scope expand naturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: building a base module-by-module on Mars lets you add colonists gradually rather than dumping a hundred characters at once. This provides pacing for introducing people and broadening the story world without overwhelming readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set expectations and end goals early with the structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the rules, endgame, or scope of the 'thing' explicit early so readers understand the stakes and can anticipate progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly establishing what the structure is (rules of a game, the countdown, how many floors, lives/abilities) gives readers a 'progress bar' and clarifies how tension will escalate. Use this to create humor, tension, and clear expectations for payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use artifacts like tarot or decks as plotting maps/spreads
rubrics_metrics.description: Repurpose tools with inherent structure (tarot spreads, card decks) to map character arcs, paths of change, or scene beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Storyteller’s Tarot spread (path of change vs way things are going) or using a tarot/deck to generate or order scenes. This offers a repeatable, varied framework for plotting and can double as brainstorming and structure at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be reflexive: develop the 'thing' to support your story
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that using a thing as structure is reflexive— you may need to expand or revise the thing so it properly supports plot, pacing, and character beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should look back at their scaffold and flesh out its details (architecture, rules, modules) to avoid shallow scaffolding. Example: Howard notes realizing his locations/modules were under-detailed and needed more work to support the scenes that used them.
